The Supreme Court on Friday declined to list separately a plea seeking recall of a split verdict on how the court should hear challenges to the 2023 law governing the appointment of the chief election commissioner and other election commissioners.

A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said the five-judge Constitution bench already constituted to decide the challenges to the law could also consider the recall application and any objection to the referral.
Advocate Prashant Bhushan asked for the recall plea to be placed before Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma, who delivered the split verdict on 23 September.
He raised an alleged conflict of interest involving Justice Sharma and pointed out that the judge was due to retire the following week.
The Chief Justice said Bhushan could raise the issue before the Constitution bench, which could consider the plea even after Justice Sharma retired.
Justice Datta took the view that a two-judge bench could decide the challenges to the law.
Justice Sharma favoured referring them to a five-judge Constitution bench because they raised significant constitutional questions.
The petitions centre on the composition of the selection panel under the 2023 law.
The panel comprises the prime minister, the leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet minister.
The petitioners object to the exclusion of the Chief Justice of India.

stories.headline: Can't imagine how Sooryavanshi will destroy bowlers at 25: Ross Taylor
stories.title: Can't imagine how Sooryavanshi will destroy bowlers at 25: Ross Taylor
stories.summary: In his 16-year international career, Ross Taylor has notched up 93 half-centuries. But he is now chasing another—his 50th visit to India. “It’s my 49th time. One more and I will raise the bat,” says one of New Zealand’s most celebrated No. 3 batters. In India as an ambassador for the New Zealand pavilion at ProWine Mumbai 2026, an alcobev trade show, Taylor spoke to Forbes India about franchise cricket versus the rest, the growth of format specialists and the relevance of ODI cricket. Edited excerpts:It was nice to be the first to play 100 games in each format. Virat Kohli was the second one to do that. But with the way cricket's going and with franchise cricket, I think less and less players will be able to play all formats and more people will become 20-20 specialists. But I hope that people can still play the game of Test cricket, because that's the ultimate. But, also, 20-20 cricket's where the money is at and the fame for these younger players. Hopefully, in time, they will still want to play Test cricket.Q. So the format is going to consume the other formats of cricket?I think so, it’s almost doing that already.Q. Is it a good thing?No, I don’t think so. Because one-day cricket is still a great format to play. But, I think, out of the three formats, that's the one that's getting consumed by the amount of franchise cricket that's going on. I’m sure, in time, it will balance itself out, but maybe World Cups are where it's at for ODI cricket. We'll have to wait and see. Cricket is moving at a fast pace—when IPL started in 2008, I don’t think anyone could have envisioned it being as big and as popular as it is now.Q. Since you mentioned the ODI World Cup, the next one is just about a year away. The Indian team was recently in New Zealand to play an ODI series and you would have seen Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma in action. Do you see them making it to the next ODI World Cup?Without a doubt. Those were very tough conditions to play in New Zealand, but Rohit and Virat, the way they were fielding, was unbelievable. You wouldn't have thought that they were 38 and going on 40. I [not only] expect them to be in the team, but they'll also dominate. I think if they do win the Cup, that's Rohit and Kohli's finale—I think they'll retire from international cricket on a high. I hope for Indian fans and world cricket that they can at least get to a final with New Zealand and may the best team win.Q. You spoke about the growth of the IPL. The player that's got all of us talking since the last season is a 15-year-old: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, who was recently in New Zealand for the T20 series. What's your assessment of his batting?Unbelievable, the fact that he's 15. My daughter's 15, and even she can’t believe it. And he's been doing it for so long as well. He started with Rajasthan Royals [RR] when he was 13. I watched video clips of him absolutely destroying bowlers in the nets. And you're thinking, he's only 15, what can he do when he's 25 and a fully grown man? At the moment, he's an amazing talent. And for Indian cricket, not only T20 cricket, I'm sure he's going to have a big future in both one-day and, hopefully, Tests as well.Q. How does he transition to a more patient approach with the red ball?At the end of the day, he just needs to play more cricket. Obviously, he's so successful in what he's doing at the moment. But once he has some more Ranji Trophy, some more [domestic cricket]... the world's ahead of him. It's really up to him whether he wants to change his game to play the longer format. But India loves its Test cricket just as much. And for him to be up there with Kohli and [Sachin] Tendulkar, [Rahul] Dravid and all the greats, he'll need to play Test cricket—and I'm sure he will in time. I’m sure we'll see his progress in the coming years.Q. He's also a very young player. How do you think his career needs to be managed?It's like anything else. You've still got to rely on your parents to guide you and make decisions for you. We saw how long a career Sachin Tendulkar had as a 16-year-old. And Sooryavanshi is even younger, so I hope he is managed well.I know Shane Bond, the bowling coach at RR, very well. He says he's a great kid. And he keeps learning and maturing every year that he's down with him. So I think it's going to be an exciting time for him. Like any cricketer, he’s going to go through ups and downs. But it's exciting to see where he can get to and how he can transform the sport.Q. He's become the captain of his state team in the domestic T20 league. Do you think it's too early or he's going to mature into the role?As I said, he's going to mature naturally in his own time. But the coaching staff and management obviously see him as a leader and having that extra responsibility, I think it's great to give it to him early on. It just sounds strange when you're talking about a 15-year-old. But he's an exciting talent. I'm sure captaincy will bring out a different side to him. And he'll learn a lot, and will put his own style on the role as well.Q. You're here at ProWine 2026 as the ambassador for New Zealand wines. You have your own wine line as well. You’ve also played T20 cricket for Samoa last year. There’s lots going on post retirement.When people ask me what I'm doing, I feel like I'm not doing a lot, but then when you pull the layers back, I'm very busy. It's great to be in India. It's my 49th time in India—one more and then I'll raise the bat [laughs].We hosted Prime Minister Narendra Modi in July this year, and it was nice to get the free trade agreement across the line. It’s also nice to bring my own wine label that is selling in New Zealand to India and hopefully fans of cricket can try the wine and enjoy it.

stories.title: Supreme Court rejects Tamil Nadu’s plea for 11 TMC of Cauvery water
stories.summary: The Supreme Court dismissed two applications seeking the release of 11 TMC of Cauvery water and said it would also dismiss a third seeking to place additional documents on record

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed two applications by Tamil Nadu seeking directions to Karnataka to release 11 thousand million cubic feet (TMC) of Cauvery water.
Tamil Nadu said the shortfall had accumulated by 7 October and asked the court to order Karnataka to make it up at Billigundulu, a water-monitoring station on the border between the two states.
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh said it would also dismiss a third application from Tamil Nadu seeking to place additional documents on record.
The court had reserved its decision on the two water-release applications on 12 October.
Tamil Nadu argued that it was entitled to a proportionate share of available river flows during a year of poor rainfall, together with water it said was already owed.
It told the court that an early kharif crop had been lost and sought interim relief to prevent further losses.
In its application, the state said the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee had assessed on 24 September that 52.935 TMC should have reached Billigundulu after accounting for the deficit in flows.
Tamil Nadu said the committee reduced the required flow from 6,000 to 4,000 cubic feet per second, or cusecs, without directing Karnataka to clear the backlog.
It also said Karnataka fell short of the 4,000-cusec requirement between 24 September and 7 October, leaving a further deficit of 0.94 TMC for that period.
Tamil Nadu argued that the subsequent reduction to 3,000 cusecs from 9 October was inadequate.
It also said the Cauvery Water Management Authority had yet to devise a formula for sharing water in years of scarcity.
Karnataka told the court that rainfall had fallen short and several areas had been declared drought-affected.

stories.headline: GMR Sports appoints Mahela Jayawardene as director of cricket for WPL
stories.title: GMR Sports appoints Mahela Jayawardene as director of cricket for WPL
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 20 : Former Sri Lanka captain Mahela Jayawardene has been appointed as Director of Cricket by GMR Sports. In this role, Jayawardene will oversee cricket operations of Delhi Capitals franchise in the Women’s Premier League (WPL), Dubai Capitals in the ILT20 and Southern Brave in The Hundred. Jayawardene will be responsible for team strategy, talent identification and the development of players and coaching staff. The appointment gives DC a heavyweight figure as they aim to finally win the WPL title. The franchise, one of the five founding WPL teams in 2023, has reached the final in all four editions of the tournament so far but finished runners-up each time. “Delhi Capitals has a strong identity and an exciting vision for the future of women’s cricket. I am delighted to take on the role of Director of Cricket for the WPL team. “The competition has enormous potential to shape the future of the women’s game, and I look forward to working with an established group of talented players and an experienced support team. “My focus will be on building on the team’s existing strengths, bringing greater consistency to performances and ensuring we continue to evolve and compete for the title. I am excited about what we can achieve together,” Jayawardene said in a statement on Saturday. Jayawardene recently left his role as head coach of Mumbai Indians, whom he coached to three IPL titles. From 2022–2024, Jayawardene was also MI’s Global Head of Performance, where he oversaw cricketing operations across franchise teams in different leagues. DC was the last team Jayawardene represented as a player in the IPL in 2012 and 2013 seasons and even captained them. Across the GMR Sports cricket teams portfolio, Jayawardene will give strategic direction on cricketing operations, talent identification, player development and performance management and work closely with the leadership, head coaches and cricket management teams at each franchise. He will also work with Giles White, Hampshire’s Director of Cricket, to share knowledge, expertise and best practices across the group’s teams. One of the finest batters of his generation, Jayawardene played 149 Tests and 448 ODIs for Sri Lanka, scoring 11,814 and 12,650 runs respectively. He captained his country and was part of the side that won the 2014 Men’s T20 World Cup. article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 20, 2026) directed the Jharkhand government to register a zero FIR in connection with a missing Bangladeshi national, who came to India in March 2025 on a medical visa and was last seen in Deoghar.
A zero FIR can be registered at any police station, irrespective of where the crime took place.

A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana was hearing a petition filed by the wife of the missing man, seeking a direction to the authorities to trace him.
The Bench observed that he was last seen in Jharkhand.
“You register a zero FIR with regard to missing person,” the Court told the counsel appearing for Jharkhand.
It also directed the State government to file a compliance report.
Counsel for the Centre told the Bench that a status report had been filed in the matter.

The West Bengal government had earlier filed a status report in the Court, saying the man entered India on March 20, 2025, through the Fulbari integrated check post on a medical visa valid until July 18, 2025, for treatment at a hospital in Siliguri.
The report said he attended the outpatient department on two dates, but was never admitted to the hospital, and there was no record of any later visits.
It said his mobile number, which he obtained locally on his passport, was active near a ‘satsang ashram’ in Deoghar on a particular date and time, but his whereabouts thereafter were not known.
The status report added that the handset was subsequently used with another SIM card by a person in Bihar.

In a separate status report filed earlier, the Jharkhand government said an inquiry was made at the ‘satsang ashram’, and no entry of the missing person or any Bangladeshi national was found for March 24-25, 2025.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 20, 2026) dismissed an appeal by the Karnataka State government challenging a State High Court decision to allow bike-taxis as public transport, removing the brakes on taxi aggregators like Ola, Uber, and Rapido from offering two-wheeler taxi services in the State.
A Bench headed by Justice Satish Chandra Sharma said regulation was better than a blanket ban.
The judge said even the staff in his office opt to travel by bike-taxi rather than autorickshaws and cabs due to the considerable fare difference.
The judge noted that bike-taxis with GPS were safer for women, and two-wheeler taxis are already operating across 25 States.
The Karnataka government had found bike-taxis dangerous, saying they were not meant for public transport, considering the low safety standards of motorcycles and higher accident fatality rates.
The State, represented by advocate Sanchit Garga, argued that the restriction on using two-wheelers as taxis was reasonable, proportionate, and in the public interest.
“The State has not imposed a blanket prohibition on the use of motorcycles for commercial purposes; rather, it has only restricted their use for carrying passengers.

Motorcycle riders continue to have viable alternative avenues of livelihood, including under the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2025, which provides statutory protection and welfare measures for such workers,” Karnataka submitted.
A Division Bench of the High Court, in January 2026, set aside a Single Bench order from April last year, which stopped bike-taxi services pending the framing of a policy by the State.

The Division Bench decision, challenged by the State in the apex court, had held that taxi aggregators and individual motorcycle owners possessed a “crystallised right to obtain permits for operating motorcycles as taxis under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988”.
The High Court had further held that motorcycles fell within the category of ‘transport vehicles’.
It directed the State authorities to positively consider applications for carriage permits for motorcycles.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court has set aside a Calcutta High Court judgment that reduced an arbitral award in favour of a dredging contractor by 50%, holding that a court exercising jurisdiction under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, cannot interfere with an award merely because the amount granted for additional work appears excessive.

The Court held that the High Court's conclusion that the claim for additional work, which exceeded 70% of the original contract value, shocked its conscience was not a legally sustainable ground for modifying the award.

A bench of Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Justice K. Vinod Chandran set aside a Calcutta High Court Division Bench order that had reduced the arbitral award by 50% on the ground that the amount awarded for additional work exceeded the original contract value by over 70%.

The Court noted that since the additional amount arose from repeated dredging undertaken by the contractor to keep the channel and basin operational, thus, the High Court had mechanically exercised its jurisdiction under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, to set aside the award on the mere ground that it exceeded the contract work value merely noting that it shocked the court's conscience without providing a “substantive reason which blatantly and patently brings forth the conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice, resulting in the conscience of the Court being shocked.”

“…the impugned order has merely used the words on the sole ground of the bills for the additional work having exceeded 70% of the original contract; without looking at the nature of the additional work involved… The Division Bench considering the application under Section 37 has not looked into the measurement or the invoices, which in any event, would be an exercise of adjudication on merits, clearly prohibited under the Act of 1996.
The measurements and invoices raised are of one character, based on the additional work of redredging which cannot be compartmentalised as 'valid' and 'invalid'.”, the Court said.

The dispute arose from a contract awarded by the Kolkata Port Trust to Marino Dredgeco for dredging the riverbed and shores at Sagar Island to create an approach channel and basin for a pilot station.
During execution, repeated dredging became necessary due to siltation, adverse weather conditions, and differences between the actual soil conditions and the data supplied by the Port Trust.
The Port Trust also entrusted additional work through a letter dated July 19, 2000.
After completing the work, the contractor raised additional bills, which led to arbitration.
The Arbitrator awarded the claimed amounts, and the Single Judge upheld the award under Section 34.

However, the High Court Division Bench, in an appeal under Section 37, reduced the amount by 50% and reduced interest, reasoning that the additional-work claims exceeded 70% of the original contract value and shocked the Court's conscience, following which an appeal was filed by the award holder, Marino Dredgeco, before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court recently directed a private school to pay Rs 10 Lakh each to two clerks as compensation for the wrongful termination of their services, noting that their case had failed in the High Court because of poor drafting of the writ petitions.
“The present case illustrates how a meritorious cause was allowed to fail by reason of inept drafting of a writ petition, the substance having been eclipsed by form.”
The appellants were proceeded against departmentally for alleged misappropriation of public money and other charges, along with the in-charge headmaster.

After an inquiry under the Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1981, in which they did not participate, the charges were held as established which led to termination of their services, however the inquiry reports were not furnished to them.
Thereafter, the appellants filed an appeal before the School Tribunal, Mumbai, which stayed the termination orders and directed the school to resume service on 50% salary.
The school challenged the order before the High Court, which allowed the school to apply to the Tribunal to lead evidence to substantiate the charges of misconduct.
However, the school never made such an application, and the Tribunal did not insist on evidence.
The Tribunal dismissed the appeals, noting that the appellants had deliberately avoided the inquiry.
It also found sufficient documentary evidence on record to deny them relief.

Subsequent to this, the appellants approached the High Court under Article 226, relying mainly on the fact that the in-charge headmaster's termination had been converted to compulsory retirement by the Tribunal, based on which they sought similar treatment.
The High Court dismissed the petitions, holding that the headmaster and the appellants did not stand on the same footing.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (November 19) held that verified PACL plot allottees in Mohali and Bhatinda who paid through banking channels are entitled to either obtain sale certificates for their plots or receive refunds with 8% interest, depending on the amount and timing of their payments.

Accepting the recommendations of the Committee, constituted to oversee the liquidation of PACL's assets and refund of investors, with certain modifications, a bench of Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Justice Atul S. Chandurkar also directed that allottees who paid less than 50% of the consideration through banking channels be refunded their verified payments with 8% interest after the concerned plots are successfully auctioned.
The dispute arose from SEBI's action against PACL for allegedly operating an unregistered Collective Investment Scheme.
In 2016, the Supreme Court constituted a committee headed by former Chief Justice of India R.M. Lodha to liquidate PACL's land assets and facilitate refunds to investors.
The Committee examined claims relating to the three residential projects and classified the allottees into five categories based on the mode and extent of payment and the timing of transactions.
The Court accepted the Committee's categorisation and recommendations, with certain modifications.
• Category I: Allottees who paid the entire consideration through banking channels will receive sale certificates/NOCs within eight weeks.
Those without possession certificates will also be issued them.
• Category II: Allottees who paid more than 50% through banking channels will be allowed to pay the outstanding amount and obtain sale certificates.
Failure to pay within the prescribed period will result in the plot being treated as unsold and the verified amount being refunded under Category III.
• Category III: Those who paid less than 50% through banking channels will receive refunds with 8% interest within three months of the successful auction of the plot.
• Category IV: Claims involving cash payments will not be processed for allotment or refund through the Committee.

stories.headline: From Kanji to Caviar: How chefs are reinventing the food they grew up eating
stories.title: From Kanji to Caviar: How chefs are reinventing the food they grew up eating
stories.summary: At his farm-to-table restaurant Farmlore in Bengaluru, Johnson Ebenezer builds dishes around storytelling. His rendition of ‘Eid’ (left) draws on the idea of breaking the fast, bringing together rose milk, a samsa (flaky pastry) cooked over a lamb bone, haleem, and a salad of nasturtiums, dates and pine nuts. The pazhya soru (right), meanwhile, features rosematta rice, a rich lobster thokku (relish), and potato-wrapped anchovies—it is a throwback to his childhood memory of watching his father, a policeman and hockey player, have breakfast with a bowl of kanji (porridge made from leftover rice), accompanied by onion, salted fish and an egg.Johnson Ebenezer was 12 when his father’s breakfast ritual caught his eye. Ebenezer senior, a policeman and a hockey player, would return home from practice around 9 every morning and settle down with a bowl of kanji—porridge made from leftover rice—alongside a few slices of onion, karuvadu (dried, salted fish) and an egg. “It’s something he would have every day while leaving aside the idlis and dosas for his three kids,” says Ebenezer.Decades later, that memory found an expression in the unlikeliest of places: A fine-dining menu. In 2021, when Ebenezer opened Farmlore—an 18-cover farm-to-table restaurant in Bengaluru—with friend Kaushik Raju, he served his rendition of fermented rice porridge. Only, this time, he paired it with lobster and topped it with potato-wrapped anchovies, in place of the simple karuvadu his father once ate. “A photograph of the dish was featured all over when we were selected for Asia’s 50 Best,” says Ebenezer, the chef co-founder of the restaurant ranked No. 83 among Asia’s top 100. “It felt like life coming full circle.”Like Ebenezer, Hussain Shahzad, named among TIME100 Next India 2026 list, grew up in Chennai, but Sunday lunches in his Bohri Muslim household meant biryani, usually cooked by mother Nafisa. He particularly eyed the khurchan—the crisp, caramelised layer of rice that stuck to the bottom of the one-pot dish—but he rarely got to enjoy it. “There was only so much to go around, and it was my brother, being the youngest, who was showered with all the love and the lion’s share,” laughs Shahzad, the executive chef of Hunger Inc Hospitality, which runs The Bombay Canteen, O Pedro, Papa’s and Veronica’s.When he designed the food programme at Papa’s—the 12-seater, ₹8,000+-per-person restaurant in Mumbai that had made it to Time magazine’s ‘The World’s Greatest Places 2025’—Shahzad dug deep into his childhood memory of sparring with his brother for the prized crust. The result was a paella-style duck biryani, with generous spoonfuls of khurchan built into it. “It means everyone can now have crunchy rice,” says Shahzad of the dish served as part of the 12-course tasting menu.Also Read: In Peru, Machu Picchu comes second to food: Chef Micha TsumuraHow Nostalgia worksLike Ebenezer and Hussain, chefs at some of India’s most premium restaurants are drawing inspiration not from the culinary canon but from uncelebrated, everyday dishes they’ve eaten, be it at home or at a roadside eatery. Rooted in childhood memories and nostalgia, the food is being reimagined and reinterpreted for the fine-dining table—with novel ingredients, meticulous techniques and aesthetic presentation elevating familiar flavours.At Masque—the Mumbai restaurant ranked India’s No. 1 and World No. 26 on the World’s 50 Best Restaurants list—city-bred chef Varun Totlani has captured in a cup the quintessential monsoon ritual of savouring bhutta (corn on the cob) with cutting chai (tea) in pouring rain.Totlani and his team have distilled the essence of this street-side favourite into a cup of corn chai, a preparation that takes three days and gets its flavour from reducing 100 litres of corn stock to just 30, then topping it with a froth made of corn miso and cream. “People don’t expect the flavour bomb when they just see a glass of tea. It’s a super hit item on the menu, and the only dish that has been carried over from previous menus,” says Totlani, of one of the highlights of the ₹9,999-per-person, 10-course degustation menu at the restaurant. Growing up in Chennai, Sunday afternoons for Hussain Shahzad, the head chef of Hunger Inc Hospitality, would mean biryani cooked by his mum Nafisa (seen in the left picture) and sparring with his younger brother for khurchan, the crisp, caramelised rice layer stuck to the bottom. At Papa’s, the 12-seater restaurant in Mumbai, Shahzad has recreated the memory with What the Duck, a duck biryani cooked like a paella, with spoonfuls of khurchan built into the dishNostalgia can also shape a restaurant’s larger culinary philosophy, influencing ideas and informing the menu.Growing up, Niyati Rao, chef-founder of Mumbai’s Ekaa—a four-star recipient in Culinary Culture’s 2026 restaurant ratings (an F&B platform co-founded by journalist Vir Sanghvi and investor Sameer Sain)—was fascinated by the art of balance in her mother’s cooking. She realised that the combination of elements on her mother’s thali—a spoonful of sabzi, a fried fish on the side, a pickle, a salad, what have you—weren’t just thrown together randomly, but assembled to bring a play of textures and flavours. “That’s why if you order an à la carte dish at Ekaa, you’ll get five different plates with it,” says Rao.For her dish that heroes mogri—green-purple radish pods available for only a few weeks in winter—Rao sources the vegetable from Mumbai’s Bhuleshwar market and pickles it to preserve it year-round.At Ekaa, she serves it over a purple yam (which she calls kand) mash, a nod to her grandmother’s kand ki sabzi that she ate with mogri during her fasts—alongside homemade sourdough crisps, tindli pickle, a warm salad, and buttermilk on the side. “It’s an old Indian philosophy that palates want a play of different flavours and textures,” says Rao. “The main ingredient may be the star of the show, but will only taste right if you pair it with the others.”Sometimes, nostalgia gives a dish a deep cultural context, weaving storytelling into every bite. Litti-chokha, a staple in nearly every Bihari household, was also a constant at every family gathering attended by Manish Mehrotra, India’s celebrated chef and culinary ambassador. But despite its emotional resonance, the dish has seldom made it to the menus of high-end restaurants, given its rustic origins—starting off as a farmer’s meal and then sold around in street carts in the state.Mehrotra decided to change that at Nisaba, his first solo venture, in Delhi’s Nizamuddin. Priced at ₹995, he serves a Bihari litti that comes with a creamy potato mash; a roasted eggplant mixed with raw onion, coriander, green chilli, ginger, garlic and mustard oil; a tomato chutney that would accompany littis at his home to cut down the heaviness of ghee; and finally, a peanut and chilli chutney that’s a nutty riff of neighbourhood stalls in Patna. “A key thing in transitioning a dish from memory to a high-end restaurant is to incorporate the ease of eating, so I have made the littis smaller,” says Mehrotra. “The dish also needs to cater to most palates—so I have toned down the use of mustard oil since its pungency may not agree with every diner.”Mehrotra’s neighbouring state, Bengal, faces a culinary conundrum of its own: A deep love for fish, coupled with the challenge of tackling the cumbersome fish head in the refined setting of a restaurant. The predicament is even greater with the golda chingri (giant freshwater prawns), whose distinctive flavour, residing in its ghilu (brains, in Bengali), needs to be sucked out. “In weddings, where the golda chingri is served, one has to find an isolated corner of the building to have the fish head in peace,” says Avinandan Kundu, the lawyer-turned-chef who runs the kitchen of Kolkata’s Sienna along with Koyel Roy Nandy. “Even in restaurants, prawn comes without the head. It’s a disservice to the memory of Bengali families enjoying the ghilu, squeezing it out on a plate of piping hot rice.”Kundu and Nandy wanted to bring that experience back to the restaurant table, and to do so, ventured beyond their regional brief. At Sienna—a fine-dining destination featured on Tatler Asia’s inaugural list of India’s 20 best restaurants—they serve the prawn with a ghilu hollandaise, a rich, creamy French sauce enriched with fat from the prawn head. “This dish was conceived to keep a memory alive on the plate,” says Kundu. At Kolkata restaurant Sienna, chefs Avinandan Kundu and Koyel Roy Nandy (right) are bringing to the table food traditions that have long remained tucked away in Bengali households. Their golda chingri (giant prawns) with ghilu hollandaise (below, left) is a nod to the families getting together for a meal and squeezing the flavourful ghilu (brain) on a plate of hot rice—a practice that was considered unfit for refined restaurant settings; (bottom right) the Horlicks ice cream, a stretchy ice cream topped with caramel to recreate the sticky residue that gathers at the bottom of a glass and is a favourite with the kidsRecipe for SuccessBut nostalgia alone doesn’t make a dish fine-dining. The transformation lies in how chefs reinterpret dishes without losing their essence. This is where one has to carefully straddle two components—form and flavour. “And you can only stretch one, not both, at the same time,” says Shahzad of Hunger Inc. “Then a dish becomes unrecognisable, and you have to do the talking to convince a diner, instead of letting your food do the talking.”At Papa’s, Shahzad serves a foie gras laddoo that resembles the Indian sweet but, stuffed with foie gras pâté and quince jam, tastes more like a foie gras bonbon. “Here, I have stayed true to the form, serving it in the shape of a motichur laddoo, while stretching the flavour, making it taste nothing like one,” he says. The approach is reversed in his lamb nihari pie, which brings together his mother’s nihari (a slow-cooked meat stew) and the classical French training he received at New York’s Eleven Madison Park. Encased in a pie, the nihari retains its familiar flavour even as its form is transformed. “Anyone who bites into it will instantly recognise the flavour,” Shahzad adds.So, invoking the familiarity of taste is central to turning a humble food memory into culinary royalty. But while familiarity may draw a diner to a dish, artfulness and reinvention make it worthy of a fine-dining menu. At Masque, the corn chai (left) and the Bombay toastie (right) are Varun Totlani’s shoutout to Mumbai, the city he grew up in. With the former, he has captured in a cup the quintessential ritual of savouring bhutta (corn on the cob) with cutting chai (tea) in Mumbai’s monsoon, while the latter is his interpretation of the chutney sandwich, the ubiquitous, inexpensive street mealAt Masque, why would diners pay nearly ₹10,000 for a 10-course menu to have, among others, a bite-sized portion of the Bombay sandwich—the ubiquitous, inexpensive street meal that often costs no more than a hundred? Because Totlani, who runs the kitchen at the feted restaurant, has invested considerable time, effort and attention to detail in recreating for the diner what a roadside vendor puts together in minutes. The beetroot pearls in Masque’s interpretation of the Bombay sandwich—to represent the slices haphazardly stacked in the original dish—are painstakingly scooped from the vegetable, cooked in the juice extracted from its trimmings, and then marinated with sumac to retain their matte finish. “Luxury dining,” says Totlani, “is never about luxury ingredients but what you do with local ingredients and how they make the diners feel.”When he was working as a chef aboard a cruise ship, Ebenezer of Farmlore once docked at Sitka, Alaska, where he sampled salmon cooked over a cider wood plank. Back at his Bengaluru restaurant, he had neither salmon nor similar wood at his disposal, but improvised with local ingredients to recreate an inspired dish: Seabass sourced from Rameswaram, marinated in mango and cooked over a mango wood plank in the wood fire. “Luxury doesn’t mean imported ingredients—it can be around you. It’s the way you treat produce with care and personalisation,” he says.Yet, ingenuity might not always convince diners to open up their purses. Kundu of Sienna had a simple answer for those who asked why he charged for a khosha bata (a traditional Bengali mash of vegetable peels), when even their mothers could make it at home. “I would tell them that if you actually had to pay your mother for the hours she’s put in the kitchen, you would find it cheaper to eat at restaurants,” he says with a laugh. “It’s surprising that these very people won’t mind paying ₹600 for a bechamel pasta, when making the bechamel sauce—a mix of flour, butter and milk—actually costs very little.”At Mumbai’s Ekaa, Rao serves a version of the fried chicken in which the meat is rendered tender through extensive brining and beating, and the dish is accompanied by an egg yolk jam, a roasted chicken bone broth, and a fermented cauliflower sambal. “The sambal is like our own XO sauce, which takes the kitchen three and a half months to make. If I don’t charge for that, what else will I charge for?” asks Rao.The tide, though, has begun to turn, particularly since Covid, as social media and ‘revenge dining’ have encouraged diners to experiment more. Only one person who’s landed up at Farmlore since its opening has ever complained about the absence of lentil and chapati on the menu. “And he was brought here for a surprise treat, so didn’t know what to expect,” laughs Ebenezer. Shahzad of Hunger Inc, too, concurs that there is growing acknowledgement of the fact that modern chefs don’t just improve an already-existing dish—say, make a better version of butter chicken—but invent forms and flavours.Ultimately, the challenge is to create a dish that feels reassuringly familiar, yet distinctive enough to cut the clutter. The real triumph of culinary nostalgia lies not in recreating the past but in giving diners something to chew on.

The tide, though, has begun to turn, particularly since Covid, as social media and ‘revenge dining’ have encouraged diners to experiment more.
Only one person who’s landed up at Farmlore since its opening has ever complained about the absence of lentil and chapati on the menu.
“And he was brought here for a surprise treat, so didn’t know what to expect,” laughs Ebenezer.

Shahzad of Hunger Inc, too, concurs that there is growing acknowledgement of the fact that modern chefs don’t just improve an already-existing dish—say, make a better version of butter chicken—but invent forms and flavours.
Ultimately, the challenge is to create a dish that feels reassuringly familiar, yet distinctive enough to cut the clutter.
The real triumph of culinary nostalgia lies not in recreating the past but in giving diners something to chew on.

sentences.text: Like Ebenezer, Hussain Shahzad, named among TIME100 Next India 2026 list, grew up in Chennai, but Sunday lunches in his Bohri Muslim household meant biryani, usually cooked by mother Nafisa.

When he designed the food programme at Papa’s—the 12-seater, ₹8,000+-per-person restaurant in Mumbai that had made it to Time magazine’s ‘The World’s Greatest Places 2025’—Shahzad dug deep into his childhood memory of sparring with his brother for the prized crust.

Growing up, Niyati Rao, chef-founder of Mumbai’s Ekaa—a four-star recipient in Culinary Culture’s 2026 restaurant ratings (an F&B platform co-founded by journalist Vir Sanghvi and investor Sameer Sain)—was fascinated by the art of balance in her mother’s cooking.

Priced at ₹995, he serves a Bihari litti that comes with a creamy potato mash; a roasted eggplant mixed with raw onion, coriander, green chilli, ginger, garlic and mustard oil; a tomato chutney that would accompany littis at his home to cut down the heaviness of ghee; and finally, a peanut and chilli chutney that’s a nutty riff of neighbourhood stalls in Patna.
